A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributive-fairness study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM experiments on allocation generation, menu selection, prompting interventions, and robustness, alongside previously published human responses.

after.justification: V2 retains original LLM experiments and adds feedback-refinement results and evaluations of Gemini-2.5-Pro.

M1.justification: V2 adds a feedback-assisted prompting procedure: a failed persona-conditioned allocation receives notion-specific corrective feedback and up to two further attempts (Appendices F.2 and J.3). The original two-stage generation and extraction procedure remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The original and synthetic allocation instances are retained. V2 adds an interactive test scenario in which models receive corrective feedback about their previous allocation, extending input conditions without introducing a new resource domain or human population.

E2.justification: Appendix H adds Gemini-2.5-Pro as an evaluated comparison model, including generation, modified-intention, explicit-equitability, and menu-selection comparisons in Tables 15–16. The original four models and additional GPT variants remain represented.

E3.justification: The new refinement experiment starts from the persona prompt and permits at most two additional attempts following failure feedback, changing the interaction protocol and response budget (Appendix F.2). The original experiments retain their stated temperature and 100-response-per-instance design.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends the diagnostic analyses: Table 11 tests whether feedback repairs failures to satisfy fairness objectives, while Table 16 contrasts a reasoning model's ability to compute equitable allocations with its generation and selection preferences. Appendix K also adds a distinct GPT-4o equitability-failure case, beyond the retained greedy-allocation error example.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly reports means with 95% confidence intervals, and Figure 5 gains error bars. Their construction is not explained. These are additions to uncertainty reporting; the PDFs do not establish an increase in independent runs.

E6.justification: Tables 11 and 15–16 add substantial findings, including Gemini-2.5-Pro's 98–100% success on explicit equitability tasks despite different menu-selection preferences. Existing Table 5 values also change: human EQ falls from 30.7% to 29.0%, and Claude-3.5S EF rises from 51.1% to 53.4%, without an explained recalculation or rerun. V1's detailed menu-selection plot and the GPT-variant comparison's I9 panel disappear.

T1.justification: The formal utility assumptions and fairness definitions are preserved between v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendix B. A limited mathematical correction expands the stated exceptions to EQ–PO incompatibility from I7 alone to I7 and I10 (v2 Section 3.4 and Appendix C.3).

C1.justification: V2's Main Results adds answer refinement to the stated contributions. The central claims about human–LLM misalignment, weak spontaneous equitability, and differences between generating and selecting allocations remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly defines alignment as agreement in prioritizing normative principles, sharpens the greedy-mechanism explanation, and interprets generation–selection differences as persisting despite enhanced reasoning. Section 6 replaces several earlier future directions with a stated data constraint on direct SFT/RLHF alignment and a proposal to train fairness-computation ability.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code/data repository pointer, API providers and model identifiers in Table 14, and complete feedback-prompt templates in Appendix J.3. These expand reproducibility documentation; the newly disclosed identifiers do not establish changes to the original experimental models.

R1.justification: The rewritten related work emphasizes normative alignment and explicitly distinguishes this study from strategic games, monetary division, and predefined allocation choices. It adds discussion of ETHICS, Delphi, Econevals, and the value–action gap, while removing v1's dedicated social-choice-and-generative-AI discussion and associated citations.

P1.justification: Related work moves into Section 1.2 and is substantially rewritten. The resource-allocation exposition and final discussion are condensed and reorganized, numbered persona/bias subsections become paragraph headings, and broader-impact and funding statements are added. These changes go beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 broadly changes typography and page composition, using wrapped and side-by-side figures and repositioned table captions. It expands Table 11, adds Tables 14–16, redraws Figure 5 with error bars, removes v1 Figure 9 and the GPT comparison's I9 panel, and adds a new error-example Figure 14.

improvement.justification: The feedback and reasoning-model experiments better distinguish computational ability from allocation preferences, while API identifiers and code/data access information improve reproducibility. The gains are limited by lost per-instance results, unexplained uncertainty calculations, and reporting inconsistencies: Table 5 changes are not propagated to nearby prose, and Appendix F.2 claims complete failure on I5 despite Table 11 reporting 10% success for GPT-4o.
